democratic.caveat: Some sampled commitments concern housing, trade, rural development, or investment generally rather than energy.
democratic.summary: Documents pair clean-energy, infrastructure, climate, manufacturing, housing, rural, and workforce investments with jobs, competitiveness, recovery, and wider economic commitments.

dsa.caveat: Some samples concern movement strategy, elections, or economic restructuring beyond energy.
dsa.summary: Documents support green transition, public investment, democratic economic control, jobs, conservation, and organizing against austerity, capitalism, and inequality.

republican.caveat: The sample also contains broader economic and national-leadership commitments.
republican.summary: Documents emphasize domestic energy supply, independence or dominance, markets, technology, trade, pipelines, deregulation, jobs, and growth, alongside some conservation or renewable measures.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Both support investment and jobs; DSA more often links transition to public ownership, democratic control, and anti-capitalist restructuring.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Democrats stress transition investment, infrastructure, climate, and jobs; Republicans more often stress supply, markets, deregulation, and energy independence or dominance.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republicans favor market-led production and supply; DSA favors public control, green transition, conservation, and democratic economic restructuring.

democratic.caveat: Programs and beneficiaries vary widely across years, so the sample is not one unified assistance plan.
democratic.summary: Documents support housing, education, health, infrastructure, income, and community-development investments directed toward low-income, rural, underserved, minority, and disaster-affected communities.

dsa.caveat: Some examples are movement priorities or broad redistributive commitments rather than program designs.
dsa.summary: Documents support preserving social programs, expanding housing and infrastructure, meeting material needs, and organizing for working-class, poor, disabled, minority, and neglected communities.

republican.caveat: Approaches range from public programs to partnerships, charities, and state-led delivery.
republican.summary: Documents support safety-net providers, veterans, foster families, local partnerships, training, transportation, child care, housing, and state or community responses to need.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Both support housing and social investment; DSA more often frames provision through working-class power, redistribution, and universal material guarantees.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Both discuss community support; Democrats more often foreground federal investment, while Republicans more often include state, charitable, family, or public-private delivery.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republicans include partnerships and decentralized delivery; DSA more often emphasizes expanded public provision, redistribution, and organizing around material needs.

democratic.caveat: Specific mechanisms and covered workers differ across platform years.
democratic.summary: Documents support unions, collective bargaining, organizing rights, higher wages, labor-law enforcement, safer workplaces, and protections for workers excluded from existing rules.

dsa.caveat: Several examples are organizing strategies or solidarity resolutions rather than legislative proposals.
dsa.summary: Documents support rank-and-file unionism, organizing, collective bargaining, strikes, labor solidarity, universal labor rights, and worker power across workplaces and social movements.

republican.caveat: The sample combines limits on union power with some worker-protection measures.
republican.summary: Documents emphasize right-to-work, secret-ballot union elections, union financial accountability, worker choice, job creation, and selected workplace or compensation protections.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Both support unions and organizing; DSA more often stresses rank-and-file power, strikes, solidarity, and broader working-class transformation.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Democrats generally favor stronger bargaining and organizing rights; Republicans more often emphasize right-to-work, secret ballots, union accountability, and worker choice.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republicans more often constrain union authority or stress individual choice; DSA emphasizes collective power, strikes, solidarity, and expansive organizing rights.

democratic.caveat: The sample mixes causal narratives, administration records, and policy commitments.
democratic.summary: Documents connect prosperity to public investment, infrastructure, manufacturing, education, inclusion, innovation, fair growth, and records attributed to Democratic administrations.

dsa.caveat: The sample spans critique, strategy, and long-term visions rather than one development program.
dsa.summary: Documents critique capitalist growth and inequality while supporting democratic planning, public investment, redistribution, labor power, and socialist alternatives organized around human needs.

republican.caveat: Some claims are retrospective or rhetorical rather than specific proposals.
republican.summary: Documents connect growth to markets, trade, lower taxes, deregulation, resource development, entrepreneurship, and economic freedom, often contrasting these with government intervention.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Democrats generally frame inclusive growth within existing institutions; DSA more often critiques capitalism and advances democratic planning, redistribution, and socialist alternatives.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Democrats more often credit investment and inclusion; Republicans more often credit markets, trade, tax reductions, deregulation, and resource development.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republicans foreground market freedom and private enterprise; DSA foregrounds capitalist inequality, public control, democratic planning, and production for human needs.

democratic.caveat: Some samples concern constitutional rights or governance beyond elections.
democratic.summary: Documents support voting-rights enforcement, restored ballot access, opposition to suppression, campaign-finance reform, representative institutions, and broader democratic accountability.

dsa.caveat: Some samples address economic democracy, public institutions, or governance rather than ballot rules.
dsa.summary: Documents support expanded voting rights, proportional representation, full democratic participation, anti-suppression measures, and limits on corporate influence over democracy.

republican.caveat: The sample mixes election administration with broader constitutional amendments and governmental limits.
republican.summary: Documents support voter identification, citizenship checks, paper ballots, state authority, representation rules, secret ballots, and selected constitutional safeguards.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Both emphasize voting access; DSA more often adds proportional representation, noncitizen enfranchisement, economic democracy, and anti-corporate structural change.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Democrats emphasize access and federal protections; Republicans more often emphasize identification, citizenship, paper ballots, state authority, and election-security rules.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republicans emphasize eligibility and ballot safeguards; DSA emphasizes expanded enfranchisement, proportional representation, participation, and restraints on corporate power.

democratic.caveat: Claims vary between national narratives, administration records, and foreign-policy commitments.
democratic.summary: Documents portray American strength through collective effort, democratic values, alliances, principled leadership, prosperity, diplomacy, and partners capable of addressing shared challenges.

dsa.caveat: Some examples concern particular wars or territories rather than a complete foreign-policy position.
dsa.summary: Documents criticize U.S. empire, military dominance, intervention, and territorial control while supporting international solidarity, self-determination, and independence for peoples under U.S. power.

republican.caveat: The sample spans aspirational rhetoric, threat narratives, and policy claims across administrations.
republican.summary: Documents portray America as an exceptional leader whose military, economy, ideals, alliances, and resolve should preserve security, freedom, prosperity, and global influence.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Democrats generally present U.S. leadership as constructive; DSA more often critiques empire, militarism, intervention, and territorial control.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Both affirm American leadership; Democrats more often stress partners and collective action, while Republicans more often stress exceptionalism, military strength, and resolve.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republicans celebrate American power and exceptional leadership; DSA challenges U.S. domination and emphasizes self-determination, solidarity, and independence.

democratic.caveat: The examples span unrelated protections and national aspirations rather than one program.
democratic.summary: Documents commit to American values, opportunity, nondiscrimination, public safety, social insurance, community strength, homeland security, and public investment.

dsa.caveat: Several examples are movement priorities or broad organizational commitments, not specific government programs.
dsa.summary: Documents support economic democratization, public investment, social movements, expanded rights, working-class organization, climate responsibility, and reduced military spending.

republican.caveat: The sample mixes domestic protections, governance, economic nationalism, and broad values.
republican.summary: Documents commit to dignity, families, efficient government, American workers, national strength, anti-discrimination enforcement, social insurance, and economic stability.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Both support protections and investment; Democrats frame institutional national commitments, while DSA more often stresses movements, economic democratization, and anti-militarism.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Both make broad protective commitments; Democrats more often emphasize opportunity and public programs, Republicans families, efficient government, and American-first priorities.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republicans emphasize national, family, and American-worker commitments; DSA emphasizes movement organizing, democratic restructuring, expanded rights, and reduced military spending.

democratic.caveat: Documents vary on trade enforcement, sanctions, military partnerships, and the balance between cooperation and unilateral action.
democratic.summary: Samples favor alliances, diplomacy, development, multilateral institutions, negotiated agreements, and international cooperation on security, trade, climate, health, and human rights.

dsa.caveat: The sample spans reformist multilateral proposals, antiwar demands, solidarity campaigns, and critiques of U.S. power.
dsa.summary: Samples support international cooperation while opposing militarism, coercive intervention, corporate trade rules, sanctions, and institutions viewed as subordinating workers or poorer nations.

republican.caveat: Positions vary across years between multilateral market opening, selective withdrawal, and stronger national control.
republican.summary: Samples combine alliances and negotiated trade with sovereignty protections, burden-sharing, firm enforcement, strategic competition, sanctions, and reservations about international courts or agreements.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Both support cooperation, but DSA samples more consistently criticize military, corporate, and coercive forms of U.S.-led international engagement.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Both discuss alliances and trade; Democratic samples stress cooperative institutions, while Republican samples more often pair engagement with sovereignty, enforcement, and strategic leverage.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republican samples more often defend strategic alliances, trade leverage, and national sovereignty; DSA samples emphasize antiwar solidarity and limits on corporate or imperial power.

democratic.caveat: Earlier documents include tougher punishment and capital punishment alongside later reform-oriented claims.
democratic.summary: Samples combine community safety and policing resources with sentencing reform, rehabilitation, reentry, civil-rights enforcement, and efforts to reduce racial disparities and excessive incarceration.

dsa.caveat: Some claims describe specific abuses or campaigns rather than a complete criminal-justice program.
dsa.summary: Samples criticize policing, prisons, criminalization, racialized violence, and punitive drug policy while supporting decarceration, abolitionist organizing, community control, and material alternatives.

republican.caveat: The sampled record varies on federal roles, sentencing, drug policy, prison reform, and capital punishment.
republican.summary: Samples emphasize public order, police support, prosecution, victims, punishment, prison administration, and local enforcement, with some attention to rehabilitation and reentry.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Democratic samples combine reform with policing institutions; DSA samples more often challenge those institutions directly and advocate decarceration or abolitionist alternatives.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Both address safety and justice administration; Democratic samples more often foreground disparity reduction and sentencing reform, while Republican samples more often emphasize enforcement and punishment.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republican samples emphasize police, prosecution, and public order; DSA samples emphasize state violence, racialized punishment, decarceration, and community-based alternatives.

democratic.caveat: Rates, thresholds, credits, and treatment of investment income vary substantially across platforms.
democratic.summary: Samples pair middle- and lower-income tax relief with credits, corporate enforcement, and higher or restored contributions from wealthy households to finance public priorities.

dsa.caveat: Documents vary between immediate revenue measures, structural redistribution, and critiques of particular tax legislation.
dsa.summary: Samples advocate progressive taxation of corporations, wealth, high incomes, estates, and financial activity to fund social programs and reduce concentrated economic power.

republican.caveat: The sampled proposals differ on credits, deductions, payroll taxes, corporate rates, and deficit implications.
republican.summary: Samples favor lower, simpler, and more predictable taxes, including relief for families, businesses, investment, estates, and savings, alongside selected enforcement measures.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Both support progressive revenue, while DSA samples more strongly frame taxation as redistribution and a challenge to concentrated corporate and wealth power.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Both propose tax relief, but Democratic samples target lower and middle incomes while seeking more corporate or affluent revenue; Republican samples favor broader rate reductions.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republican samples prioritize lower taxes for families, investment, and business; DSA samples prioritize higher taxation of wealth, corporations, and financial activity.

democratic.caveat: Documents vary on testing, charters, discipline, federal standards, and the balance between access and accountability.
democratic.summary: Samples emphasize public investment, broad access, teachers, achievement gaps, accountability, safe schools, early learning, and affordable pathways through college.

dsa.caveat: The sample combines national policy, local campaigns, organizational education, and critiques of privatization.
dsa.summary: Samples treat education as a public good, supporting universal access, public funding, democratic control, labor rights, inclusion, and reduced market or debt burdens.

republican.caveat: The record also includes public-school support, disability access, teacher policy, and federal accountability measures.
republican.summary: Samples emphasize parental choice, local control, standards, discipline, charters, vouchers, homeschooling, skills, and alternatives for students in failing schools.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Both favor access and public investment; DSA samples more explicitly oppose privatization and frame education as a universal right under democratic control.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Democratic samples emphasize public investment and equitable access; Republican samples more strongly emphasize parental choice, local control, discipline, and alternative providers.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republican samples emphasize parental choice and decentralized options; DSA samples emphasize universal public provision, labor rights, inclusion, and reduced market control.

democratic.caveat: Specific legal, funding, religious-liberty, and family-policy formulations change across years.
democratic.summary: Samples support reproductive autonomy, abortion and contraception access, gender and LGBTQ equality, family protections, caregiving, and enforcement against discrimination and violence.

dsa.caveat: The sampled documents mix programmatic demands, historical analysis, solidarity statements, and critiques of both major parties.
dsa.summary: Samples frame reproductive freedom, gender and sexual liberation, healthcare access, childcare, and freedom from violence as connected social and economic rights.

republican.caveat: The packet also contains protections for women and families that do not resolve its internal policy tensions.
republican.summary: Samples emphasize fetal life, abortion restrictions, conscience protections, traditional marriage or sex classifications, adoption, family formation, and opposition to public abortion funding.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Both support reproductive and gender equality, while DSA samples more explicitly connect those rights to socialist, labor, healthcare, and anti-capitalist demands.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Democratic samples defend reproductive and LGBTQ rights; Republican samples emphasize fetal life, conscience, traditional family definitions, and restrictions on abortion funding or access.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republican and DSA samples sharply diverge on abortion, gender, sexuality, and family law, though both sometimes discuss material support for families.

democratic.caveat: Approaches vary by conflict and administration, including disagreements over Iraq, Afghanistan, drones, detention, and defense resources.
democratic.summary: Samples combine counterterrorism, intelligence, alliances, military readiness, nonproliferation, veterans' support, and selective force with diplomacy, oversight, and ending particular wars.

dsa.caveat: Some documents address specific conflicts or solidarity campaigns rather than a comprehensive security doctrine.
dsa.summary: Samples oppose war, occupation, military intervention, nuclear escalation, surveillance, and expansive defense spending while supporting demilitarization, diplomacy, and antiwar organizing.

republican.caveat: The record varies on nation-building, alliances, treaties, war management, and the scale or purpose of deployments.
republican.summary: Samples emphasize military strength, readiness, missile and nuclear defense, counterterrorism, intelligence, support for troops, and preserving force options against identified threats.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Democratic samples retain military and intelligence tools; DSA samples more consistently reject intervention, occupation, militarized counterterrorism, and expansive defense spending.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Both support security capacity and troops; Republican samples more consistently stress force readiness, while Democratic samples more often pair security measures with diplomacy and oversight.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republican samples emphasize deterrence, readiness, and force options; DSA samples emphasize demilitarization, antiwar organizing, disarmament, and opposition to intervention.

democratic.caveat: Targets and policy fields change across elections; criticism should not be read as one unified governing program.
democratic.summary: Samples criticize Republican administrations and policies across war, economics, rights, environment, governance, and public services while sometimes pairing objections with alternative commitments.

dsa.caveat: The evidence mixes U.S. policy critiques, international solidarity, organizational analysis, and statements about particular political actors.
dsa.summary: Samples criticize Democratic and Republican administrations, capitalism, militarism, austerity, policing, intervention, and institutional failures while advancing socialist or movement-based alternatives.

republican.caveat: The sampled objections span unrelated domains and include both institutional principles and campaign-era partisan judgments.
republican.summary: Samples reject Democratic administrations, federal expansion, spending, judicial or executive actions, international constraints, military cuts, and selected trade, social, or security policies.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Democratic samples mostly oppose Republican governance; DSA samples also criticize Democratic administrations and connect policy failures to capitalism, militarism, or movement strategy.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Both criticize opposing administrations across many fields; their samples differ mainly in the policies, institutions, and governing choices they identify as failures.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republican samples object to federal expansion and Democratic governance; DSA samples object to capitalism, militarism, coercive institutions, and both major parties.

democratic.caveat: Claims span prospective promises and retrospective assessments across multiple administrations and policy fields.
democratic.summary: Samples praise Democratic presidential achievements and commitments while criticizing Republican administrations across economics, rights, war, health, environment, infrastructure, governance, and alliances.

dsa.caveat: Several samples concern foreign leaders or movements, illustrating the cluster's broad actor-centered attribution.
dsa.summary: Samples assess presidential and governmental records through socialist critiques of war, austerity, immigration, policing, intervention, corporate power, and Democratic Party limitations.

republican.caveat: The record combines campaign promises, institutional claims, and retrospective assessments from several presidencies.
republican.summary: Samples praise Republican presidential leadership and commitments while criticizing Democratic administrations on defense, borders, economics, executive authority, regulation, crime, and global instability.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Democratic samples defend Democratic presidential records; DSA samples more often criticize those administrations from antiwar, labor, immigrant-rights, or anti-capitalist perspectives.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Each party credits its presidents and faults the other's administrations across many policy domains, producing contrasting leadership records rather than one substantive disagreement.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republican samples praise conservative presidential leadership; DSA samples criticize U.S. administrations, including Trump, through antiwar, socialist, and international-solidarity frames.

democratic.caveat: Proposals vary by year across universal coverage, insurance expansion, public programs, providers, and cost controls.
democratic.summary: Sampled platforms seek broad affordable coverage, stronger Medicare and Medicaid, lower costs, prescription access, public-program equity, and reduced disparities across communities and territories.

dsa.caveat: Some examples address adjacent reproductive care, addiction, institutions, immigration status, or specific reform campaigns.
dsa.summary: Sampled documents treat healthcare as a right and favor Medicare for All, single-payer coverage, public investment, universal eligibility, comprehensive benefits, and care without point-of-use charges.

republican.caveat: The samples include both program protection and restructuring, with varied approaches to coverage and regulation.
republican.summary: Sampled platforms support affordable access through choice, competition, consumer control, targeted credits, Medicare and Medicaid changes, community care, prevention, and private provision.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Democratic samples expand mixed-system coverage; DSA samples more consistently demand universal single-payer or publicly guaranteed care without financial barriers.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Both seek affordable access; Democratic samples emphasize coverage expansion and public guarantees, while Republican samples more often emphasize choice, competition, and consumer control.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republican samples emphasize private options, competition, and targeted programs; DSA samples emphasize universal public financing, single-payer design, and healthcare as a right.

democratic.caveat: These are mainly problem descriptions; sampled remedies and causal explanations vary by document and year.
democratic.summary: Documents describe poverty, job loss, housing unaffordability, racial wealth gaps, health costs, disaster burdens, and pandemic-era fiscal strain across successive election periods.

dsa.caveat: Some examples concern foreign humanitarian crises or broad systemic diagnoses rather than U.S. household insecurity alone.
dsa.summary: Documents connect hardship to low wages, austerity, weak labor standards, privatization, capitalism, housing costs, incarceration, and crises, emphasizing burdens on workers and marginalized communities.

republican.caveat: Samples combine household hardship, macroeconomic indicators, and international poverty without one consistent causal theory.
republican.summary: Documents describe poverty, uninsured families, housing collapse, inflation, trade deficits, unemployment, health disparities, and fiscal distress, sometimes assigning partisan or public-cost blame.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Both describe hardship and unequal burdens; DSA more consistently attributes them to capitalism, austerity, weakened labor standards, privatization, and incarceration.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Both document poverty, housing, employment, and cost pressures; Republican samples more often attach partisan or fiscal blame, while Democratic samples emphasize inequality and disparate burdens.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republicans mix household hardship with trade and fiscal critiques; DSA emphasizes low wages, austerity, capitalist development, and diminished public services.

democratic.caveat: Examples span domestic and foreign actors, historical injustices, security threats, labor, technology, and civil rights.
democratic.summary: Documents describe threats from criminal networks, authoritarian regimes, discrimination, anti-worker conduct, political violence, technology abuse, and institutions that undermine rights or democracy.

dsa.caveat: Examples range across international conflict, migration, labor struggles, political violence, and broad systemic critique.
dsa.summary: Documents link oppression and social conflict to capitalism, racism, austerity, anti-labor politics, police, prisons, borders, surveillance, militarism, and elites dividing working people.

republican.caveat: The sample combines international human rights, domestic institutions, regulation, taxation, education, and partisan rhetoric.
republican.summary: Documents describe threats from foreign repression, criminal trafficking, government overreach, corruption, judges, ideological institutions, and policies portrayed as weakening freedom, markets, or order.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Both criticize discrimination, violence, and attacks on workers; DSA more consistently roots them in capitalism, class power, borders, policing, and prisons.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Both identify threats to rights and democracy; Democratic samples emphasize discrimination and authoritarianism, while Republican samples more often emphasize government overreach and institutional corruption.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republican samples often portray government and ideological institutions as coercive; DSA samples portray capitalist, carceral, border, and right-wing institutions as oppressive.

democratic.caveat: The balance between legalization, humanitarian protections, and enforcement changes substantially across election years.
democratic.summary: Platforms combine pathways to citizenship, family reunification, asylum and immigrant protections with border security, employer enforcement, screening, and administrative reform.

dsa.caveat: Some samples discuss particular bills, foreign asylum disputes, trafficking, healthcare, or organizing campaigns rather than comprehensive policy.
dsa.summary: Documents support citizenship, asylum, immigrant labor rights, free movement, abolition of ICE, demilitarized borders, and ending detention, deportation, and punitive immigration controls.

republican.caveat: Earlier reform and service proposals coexist with increasingly expansive detention, deportation, and border-enforcement commitments.
republican.summary: Platforms welcome legal immigration while emphasizing border control, enforcement, screening, detention or removal, employer and smuggling penalties, national interest, and lawful citizenship processes.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Both support legalization and immigrant protections; DSA samples more consistently reject detention, deportation, ICE, militarized borders, and restrictive controls.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Both include legal pathways and enforcement; Democratic samples emphasize citizenship and humanitarian protections, while Republican samples increasingly prioritize border control, detention, and removal.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republican samples emphasize enforcement, screening, borders, and removal; DSA samples emphasize free movement, amnesty, asylum, abolition of ICE, and ending detention and deportation.

democratic.caveat: Emphasis shifts by conflict and administration; security support coexists with humanitarian aid and Palestinian self-determination.
democratic.summary: Platforms combine Israeli security with Palestinian statehood, assistance, diplomacy, negotiated peace, and, by 2024, ceasefire and Gaza reconstruction language.

dsa.caveat: Samples also include Iraq, Syria, Yemen, antisemitism, and other regional or antiwar claims outside Israel-Palestine.
dsa.summary: Documents emphasize Palestinian sovereignty, return, self-determination, ending occupation and military aid, ceasefires, and solidarity, while earlier samples sometimes endorse negotiated two-state peace and Israeli civilian security.

republican.caveat: The lone 2024 sample is broad; most detailed Israel-Palestine positions come from 2000–2016 platforms.
republican.summary: Platforms emphasize Israel’s security, diplomatic recognition, regional peace, defensible borders, and opposition to hostile groups, alongside recurring conditional support for Palestinian statehood.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Democratic samples combine Israeli security with Palestinian statehood and assistance; DSA samples more fundamentally challenge occupation, military aid, and restrictions on Palestinian sovereignty.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Both support Israeli security and negotiated peace; Democratic samples more consistently include Palestinian assistance and self-determination, while Republican samples foreground Israel and conditional statehood.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republican samples foreground Israel’s security and hostile groups; DSA samples foreground Palestinian rights, ending occupation and aid, return, ceasefire, and antiwar politics.

democratic.caveat: Claims span campaign warnings and retrospective accusations from 2016–2024, not independently adjudicated findings.
democratic.summary: Platforms criticize Trump on alliances, diplomacy, labor, trade, pandemic response, health and social programs, immigration, climate, racial equity, political violence, and democratic norms.

dsa.caveat: Samples mix policy criticism, attributed rhetoric, protest appeals, and predictions about a second Trump term.
dsa.summary: Documents criticize Trump’s immigration, racial, gender, labor, tax, environmental, foreign-policy, and militarist record, while describing movement growth and opposition during his presidency.

republican.caveat: Only one 2016 claim appears, and it criticizes an unnamed president rather than documenting Trump’s record.
republican.summary: Samples, chiefly from 2024, praise Trump’s trade, energy, manufacturing, border, Medicare, national-pride, and economic record while promising renewed implementation.

democratic_vs_dsa.summary: Both criticize Trump across foreign and domestic policy; DSA more often frames those harms through capitalism, working-class struggle, militarism, and movement organizing.

democratic_vs_republican.summary: Democrats describe Trump as damaging alliances, rights, services, and democratic norms; Republicans praise his economic, energy, border, and national leadership, chiefly in 2024.

republican_vs_dsa.summary: Republican documents celebrate Trump’s leadership and policy record; DSA documents depict his administration and movement as threats to workers, marginalized groups, peace, and social provision.
